title: Your Obligation Remains the Same
author: Ryan Holiday
summary: Written in the days after a U.S. election, this Daily Stoic meditation argues that no election result changes the job asked of you. The author grants that elections matter, but insists that for a Stoic nothing in them alters what is obligated of a person: whether a philosopher king or a tyrant comes to power, and whether you gain power or are rendered powerless, you are still expected to be good and to act with virtue. He draws on Marcus Aurelius, who describes being bound to the good whatever anyone does or says, and on the senator Helvidius Priscus, who told the Emperor Vespasian he would keep speaking what he thought right even under threat of death. The point is that consequences, costs and stakes can change while the duty to be good, wise, courageous and resistant to evil remains. The piece ends with a simple instruction to do it, like a Stoic.
points: Elections matter, but they do not change the personal obligation to act with virtue, whether one gains power or is rendered powerless.
Marcus Aurelius is cited as describing himself as bound to the good whatever anyone does or says, with the image of an emerald showing its true colors.
The story of Helvidius Priscus answering Vespasian shows duty held under a threat of death: you do your part and I will do mine.
Stakes and costs may change with circumstances, but the duty to be good, wise and resistant to wrong stays constant.
quotes: You are not wrong to think about this. But you are mistaken if you think what has happened, what will happen or who was elected changes your job.

It doesn’t matter if a philosopher king or a tyrant comes to power, it doesn’t matter if you yourself are the person who comes to power or if you have just been rendered powerless–you are still expected to be good.
Whatever anyone does or says, for my part I’m bound to the good,” Marcus Aurelius writes in Meditations.
It is in your power not to allow me to be a member of the senate,” Helvidius replied, “but so long as I am, I must go in…and I must say what I think right.
You will do your part,” Helvidius said with immense courage, “and I will do mine.
Our job today and tomorrow is the same as it’s always been—to be good, to be wise, to stand up for what’s right, to resist what is wrong and evil.
The consequences and the costs and the stakes can change, but the obligation remains. The duty remains.
